Your response was: "I mean... I looked through it. There were some parts that felt familiar, some that didn't quite. Something about the way the options were presented felt a bit mixed up to me. I couldn't say much more than that without thinking about it more."

We want to understand what you meant by "something about the way the options were presented felt a bit mixed up to me", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The visual hierarchy of the two large buttons at the bottom, where the "Continue Shopping" button appears more prominent than the "Place Order" button.
B) The visual emphasis of the items in the "Order Summary" section, where the price for the "Wireless Mouse" appears bolder than the "Ergonomic Chair" price.
C) The grouping of the "Order Summary" and "Payment Details" sections, which might feel unclear in their vertical stacking.
D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to)

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
turns.a: A) The visual hierarchy of the two large buttons at the bottom, where the "Continue Shopping" button appears more prominent than the "Place Order" button.

turns.q: In what situation does 'Continue Shopping' looking more prominent than 'Place Order' on this layout become a problem?
turns.a: I'm not sure I have one specific moment in mind. It's more of a... recurring thing, I suppose. When the team needs to process something quickly and there's not much time for figuring out the interface. Though I'm not sure that's specific enough.

turns.q: What were you trying to verify about the intended workflow when looking at how those two buttons are visually weighted against each other?
turns.a: I suppose just... confirm which button was the main one. I don't usually think of it as a 'job' — it's more like the last step in something larger. Getting to the confirmation on the first attempt — not ending up somewhere I didn't mean to. That's the key part. When you're placing something on behalf of a group, ending up on the wrong page because the wrong option looked right means starting over, and that costs more than just your own time.

turns.q: What would the visual hierarchy between 'Place Order' and 'Continue Shopping' need to look like so the main button is unmistakable at a glance?
turns.a: "Something visible and conventional. 'Place Order' as a filled button — a real background color, not an outline. 'Continue Shopping' as text or a ghost outline — no fill, clearly subordinate. The contrast between the two is what communicates which is the action and which is the option. It doesn't have to be dramatic. It just has to be legible as a hierarchy. Right now the hierarchy is backwards. That's the standard being violated and the fix is straightforward."

turns.q: Looking at how "Place Order" is currently drawn, which specific visual attribute—its fill style, border treatment, color value, or contrast against the background—is causing it to lose prominence over "Continue Shopping"?
turns.a: 'Place Order' was styled as if it were the main action — more visual weight, more presence on the page than I'd expect for a button that takes you forward. 'Continue Shopping' — the actual thing I needed to do — looked secondary by comparison. That's the barrier. The fix: downgrade 'Continue Shopping' to a ghost button or a text link, something that reads as optional. And give 'Place Order' a solid fill color with real contrast so it's unmistakably the primary action. If those two things were right — 'Continue Shopping' quiet, 'Place Order' prominent — I'd have known immediately which was the right one without any hesitation.
